label: Suspected multiple sclerosis
note: The patient presented with jaw pain, left arm numbness, and tingling in fingertips. She reported a recent viral illness and boxing injuries. She takes ibuprofen, vitamin D, and melatonin. Her father has hypothyroidism and autoimmune conditions; her mother has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol. The patient had transient left eye vision loss and mild left-sided arm weakness. No diagnosis was made. An urgent neurology referral was arranged for brain scanning. The patient was advised to return to A&E if weakness worsens or visual symptoms progress.
patient:
Your appointment today
You came because of jaw pain. You also had arm numbness and tingling. You said you had a recent viral illness. You also had boxing injuries in the past.

Your diagnosis
We have not made a diagnosis yet.

Your treatment and next steps
We arranged an urgent referral to neurology. You will have a brain scan soon. Take your ibuprofen, vitamin D and melatonin. Rest well and do not drive yourself.

When to contact us
Call us if your arm weakness gets worse. Call us if your vision problems get worse.
summary: A patient in their forties presented with left arm numbness and tingling, mild weakness, and transient visual loss following a viral illness. Examination showed no neck pain or neurological deficits. Urgent neurology referral for brain imaging was arranged for suspected multiple sclerosis.

answers.happened: A weeks-old episode of lost vision in one eye that the patient had put down to a cold, mentioned almost in passing while we were talking about a new exercise class. Together with the numbness and weakness in one arm it changed the picture from a training strain to something needing an urgent neurology referral.
answers.learned: The history that matters can arrive as an aside. When a patient offers an odd symptom they have already explained away, stop and go back to it before moving on. Naming multiple sclerosis frightened her, and I had not prepared her for the possibility before saying the word.
answers.next: I would raise the referral first and the possible diagnosis second, and say plainly that the referral is to find out, not because I am sure. I would also give the emergency signs before the shock lands, not after, so they are heard.
